transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, it's... it's hard to explain exactly, but I suppose what brings me in is this feeling I've been having lately. I've been waking up with this just... this incredibly heavy, hollow sadness. It’s strange because I’m usually so full of energy, you know, being a choreographer, I’m constantly moving, constantly creating, constantly listening to the rhythm of things. But lately, it’s like... it's like the studio lights are on, they're glaring down at me, the mirrors are all clean, everything is set up perfectly, but there’s just no music in me anymore. Not a single note. I just stand there in the center of the room and I feel entirely empty. And it’s not just in the studio, it’s the moment I open my eyes in the morning. I just lie there in bed and the weight of it is physical, like a lead blanket pressing down on my chest, making it hard to even breathe sometimes, let alone get up and face the dancers who are expecting me to have all the answers and all the counts ready for them. I try to push through it, I really do, but this sadness, it just clings to me. It's just so heavy and so hollow, all at the exact same time.
Have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy, such as choreography or dancing?

Loss of interest? No, no, I don't think that's it at all. Actually, it's incredibly frustrating because my mind still completely revolves around dance. It's not like the passion just evaporated. 

Just the other day, I was sitting on the floor of the studio—well, I was supposed to be demonstrating a sequence—and I was looking at my lead dancer, Maya, and I could see exactly how her lines should look, how the arc of her arm needed to catch the spotlight, and I *wanted* to get up and show her. I still have all that love for it, you know? I still feel that spark when I hear a piece of music that has a really complex, driving cello part, or I'll still spend hours sketching out stage formations in my notebook because I just can't stop thinking about the geometry of the bodies on stage. I love it just as much as I did when I was getting my degree, maybe even more now. 

So, no, the interest hasn't faded even a fraction of a percent. The pleasure of creating is still something I desperately want. It's more like... the desire is completely intact, burning right there in my chest, but it's trapped under that lead blanket I was telling you about. I still want to do it all, I really, really do, I just... I physically feel like I can't bridge the gap between wanting to do it and actually getting my body to move and do it. Does that make sense? Because honestly, if I just didn't care anymore, I think this would be a lot easier to deal with, but I care so much it actually hurts.
Have you noticed that you're feeling unusually tired or lacking energy, even if you haven't been physically active?

Oh, completely. But it’s... it’s not a normal kind of tired. You know, normally, if we’re in tech week and I’m on my feet for twelve, fourteen hours a day, running numbers, shouting over the music, I get tired, sure. But that’s a satisfying tired. You sleep, you wake up, you do it again. This is... this is entirely different. I haven't been physically active at all, really. 

I mean, I have this ankle brace on right now—I just tweaked it stepping off a riser a little while ago, nothing major, just a really stupid misstep, honestly—but even just dealing with normal daily things with it is exhausting. Like, just taking a shower. I have to figure out how to navigate the tub, take the brace off carefully, and by the time I’m done just washing my hair and I step out, I am completely wiped out. I literally have to sit on the edge of the bathtub for twenty minutes just staring at the bathmat because I don't have the physical energy to even dry off. 

And it’s not just physical things, it's the smallest mental tasks, too. Yesterday, I knew I needed to reply to one of my dancers about a wardrobe fitting. Just one email. One single email to confirm a time for the seamstress. I opened my laptop, typed maybe three sentences, hit send, and I felt like I had just run back-to-back dress rehearsals. My brain just felt like mush. I was so drained I had to go lie down immediately. 

But the worst part—and this is what’s driving me crazy—is that lying down doesn’t even do anything. It doesn't recharge me at all. I'll go to bed and just lie there for hours, hoping my battery will refill, but it’s like the charger is broken. I just lie there feeling that heavy blanket I mentioned, and when I finally force myself to sit back up, I’m exactly as exhausted as I was before I lay down. It’s like the tiredness is just baked into my bones right now, and resting doesn't touch it.
Have you noticed any difficulty concentrating or thinking clearly lately, even when trying to do simple things like reading an email or following a conversation?

Concentrating? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my brain is definitely tired, like I said, but it's not like I can't focus when I really need to. It's more of an energy issue than a focus issue. 

Like, if I'm sitting there looking at my notebook, trying to map out a new sequence, I can still see the whole stage in my head. I can picture exactly where every dancer needs to be, how the lighting should hit them, the exact timing of the music... all of that is still crystal clear. I can hold the entire production in my mind without losing the thread of it. It's just that I don't have the physical drive to actually get up and execute it. 

And conversations, no, I can follow them just fine. Even when my dancers are all talking at once, asking about counts or spacing, I can still track who is saying what. It's just that responding to them feels like lifting a boulder. But the actual comprehension, the ability to think through a problem or read an email, that's all still there. It's just... it's like the engine is running perfectly fine, but there's absolutely no gas in the tank to make the car actually move forward. So, no, I don't feel confused or scattered or anything like that. Just... unbelievably drained.
Have you ever experienced a period of time when you felt unusually energetic, overly confident, or needed less sleep, maybe even to the point of feeling restless or irritable?

Energetic? Oh, God, yes. It’s... it’s actually almost painful to think about right now because of how heavy and drained I feel today, but yes, absolutely. 

There was a stretch, not even that long ago, where I just felt... dazzlingly alive. I mean, completely electric. It was like every single nerve ending was awake and vibrating with ideas. I’d be up at two, three in the morning, pacing my apartment, sketching out staging, listening to the same eight bars of a Stravinsky piece over and over because I was just so completely dialed into the music. I was getting maybe two hours of sleep a night, if that, and I didn't even care. I didn't need it. I’d walk into the studio the next morning feeling invincible, like I could physically lift the entire company on my shoulders and carry them to opening night. I was so incredibly confident about what we were building.

But... the irritable part. Yeah, that definitely happened, too, and it was intense. Because I had this massive, crystal-clear vision, right? I was moving at a million miles an hour, and my brain was ten steps ahead of everyone else in the room. And then someone—usually my assistant director, or even Maya, my lead—would try to slow me down. They’d question the plan, ask if a sequence was too ambitious for the corps, or, worse, they’d look at my foot and remind me that my ankle still needed rest. 

Because I had already tweaked it by then, you know, and I was supposed to be taking it easy, but I just couldn't. And when they would bring it up? I would get suddenly, unbelievably furious. Like, white-hot, blindingly angry. I mean, how dare they interrupt the flow, you know? I was creating something brilliant, I was finally firing on all cylinders, and they wanted me to sit on a folding chair with an ice pack? It felt like they were trying to sabotage the entire production just because of a minor sprain. I would snap at them, yell even, which isn't normally my management style at all. I usually pride myself on being so collaborative and open to feedback. But during that time, if anyone even hinted that I should take a break, or questioned a transition I was setting, or tried to baby me about the ankle, I just lost it on them. I couldn't tolerate anything or anyone slowing me down when I felt that alive. It was like they were throwing water on a grease fire.
How long have you been feeling this way with the heavy sadness and lack of energy?

Oh, wow. Um... it feels like forever, to be honest. But if I really sit down and trace it back, look at the calendar... it’s been about nine months. Yeah, nine months. 

I remember exactly when it started to really settle in, because we were just wrapping up the spring showcase. Usually, after a big run like that, I’ll take a week off, you know? I’ll sleep for three days, maybe just stay in my apartment and do nothing, and then I’m bouncing right back, completely ready to start choreographing the next piece. But this time... I took my week off, and I just never bounced back. The heaviness just arrived and decided to stay. 

I kept telling myself, "Okay, just give it another week, you're just burnt out, rest a little more." But weeks turned into months. We went through our entire summer intensive program, and I was just dragging myself into the studio every single day, sitting in the corner chair with my coffee, feeling like I was moving underwater. And then fall hit, and we started auditions for the winter gala, and I was still just... so incredibly sad and drained. It’s wild to actually say it out loud and realize it’s been three-quarters of a year. Nine whole months of just waking up and feeling like gravity has doubled. 

It's just so frustrating because, like I said before, my mind knows what needs to be done. I can see the choreography, I can envision the stage, but my mood has just been stuck in this thick mud for nine months now. I keep waiting for the fog to lift, hoping I'll wake up and feel normal again, but it just hasn't happened. Nine months is a really long time to feel like a ghost in your own studio, you know? It just drags on and on, and you start to wonder if it's ever going to end.
